title: Whose Clock Is It: Simulated Time, Jumps and the Timer That Fires 200 Times at Once

questions.question: A simulator is paused and a node keeps commanding the robot. What went wrong?
options: The simulator's pause message was lost on a best effort topic, so the node never heard it
The node's control loop is too slow to notice a pause shorter than its period
The node was started before the simulator and so has an earlier epoch
Its timer follows the wall clock and not the simulator's: a timer on the clock that stood still fired 0 times in 1000 polls
questions.explanation: When the simulator stops, its clock stops. A node that times itself by the wall clock carries on, commanding a robot that is no longer being simulated.

questions.question: A timer of period 0.5 s runs on a clock at 10 times speed. How often does it fire per clock second and per wall second?
options: 20 per clock second and 2 per wall second
2 per clock second and 20 per wall second: per clock second it is the same at every speed
2 per clock second and 2 per wall second: a timer's period is in wall time
0.2 per clock second and 2 per wall second
questions.explanation: The period is in the clock's seconds, so the count per clock second does not change. Per wall second it scales with the speed, which is where fast simulation meets the machine's limits.

questions.question: The clock jumps forward 100 s over a 0.5 s period. What should the timer do?
options: Fire 200 times at once, so that no period is missed
Not fire at all until the clock has run another 100 s
Stop, and wait to be restarted by the node
Fire a bounded number of times and count the rest as skipped
questions.explanation: Once, with 199 skipped, where a catch-up timer fired 200 times at once. The 200 overdue periods are for time that was skipped, not lived through. One firing, a count of what was skipped, and then on from the new time.

questions.question: The clock goes from 100 s back to 0. What does a timer with its old schedule do?
options: Is silent for the first 100 s of the new run
Fires 199 times at once to catch up with the new run
Fires as usual: a timer only looks at differences in time
Fires at twice its rate until it reaches its old next time
questions.explanation: It waits for the clock to reach its old next time: 0 firings against 199. Its next firing was set for 100.5 s. Unless it notices the new epoch, it sits waiting for a time the new run will not reach for a hundred seconds.

questions.question: Is a time of 1.4999 arriving after 1.5 a jump back?
options: No: a step back smaller than a millisecond is treated as noise
Only if it is followed by a second step back
Yes: any step back counts, however small, while the same time twice or a small step forward does not
No: only a step back of a whole period counts
questions.explanation: A clock that has gone back at all has started again, and timers must re-arm. A repeated time or a small step forward is ordinary.

questions.question: What does a jump back do to a lifespan or a lease remembered from before it?
options: It extends them by the size of the jump
Nothing: they are measured in wall time
It invalidates them: anything stamped in the future of the new time needs to be told, since the clock they measured against has gone back
It shortens them to zero, so every message expires at once
questions.explanation: A message stamped at 100 s is in the future once the clock reads 0. Ages and leases worked out against the old time mean nothing now.
